# The setting

Early oncology trials increasingly randomize patients to several dose
levels and look for the dose that balances efficacy, toxicity and
tolerability rather than the maximum tolerated dose.  CUI-MET (Zhang,
Broglio, Sweeting and D'Angelo 2025, arXiv:2505.03633) summarizes each
binary endpoint by its probability at each dose, combines the
probabilities with weights into a clinical utility index (CUI), and uses a
bootstrap to show how sure the choice of dose is.  `cuiDoseResponse()`
implements it.

# A simulated trial

Thirty patients at each of five dose levels, with the probabilities of the
paper's example 1.  Toxicity is undesirable, so it enters the CUI as one
minus its probability.

```{r data}
truth <- data.frame(dose = 1:5,
                    tox = c(0.038, 0.058, 0.106, 0.232, 0.533),
                    eff = c(0.022, 0.119, 0.343, 0.568, 0.681),
                    tol = c(0.147, 0.206, 0.280, 0.368, 0.466))
set.seed(2025)
trial <- truth[rep(1:5, each = 30), ]
trial$id <- seq_len(nrow(trial))
for (v in c("tox", "eff", "tol")) trial[[v]] <- rbinom(nrow(trial), 1, trial[[v]])
head(trial)
```

# Observed rates

The simplest estimate is the observed rate at each dose.  The bootstrap
resamples whole patients within each dose, so a patient's three outcomes
stay together.

```{r empirical}
empirical := cuiDoseResponse(trial,
  list(cuiBinary(tox, direction = "lower"), cuiBinary(eff), cuiBinary(tol)),
  dose = dose, id = id, weights = c(tox = 0.2, eff = 0.5, tol = 0.3),
  nBoot = 1000, seed = 1, cacheDir = NA)
empirical
```

# Dose-response models

Rates at neighboring doses inform each other when a dose-response model is
fit.  As in the paper's table 1: an exponential model for toxicity, a
logistic quadratic for efficacy and a logistic line for tolerability.  The
models are refit in each of the 1000 bootstrap samples.

```{r modeled}
modeled := cuiDoseResponse(trial,
  list(cuiBinary(tox, model = "exponential", direction = "lower"),
       cuiBinary(eff, model = "logitQuadratic"),
       cuiBinary(tol, model = "logitLinear")),
  dose = dose, id = id, weights = c(tox = 0.2, eff = 0.5, tol = 0.3),
  nBoot = 1000, seed = 1, cacheDir = NA)
modeled
```

The fitted curves, with the observed rates and the bootstrap intervals of
the fitted probabilities:

```{r dose-response, fig.height = 3.8}
plot(modeled, "doseResponse")
```

The CUI is the line, its 95% bootstrap interval the band, and the
recommended dose is marked:

```{r cui}
plot(modeled)
```

The endpoints behind it, each as a desirability with its own band:

```{r endpoints}
plot(modeled, "endpoints")
```

How often each dose has the highest CUI across the bootstrap samples:

```{r selection}
plot(modeled, "selection")
```

# Another weighting scheme

The weights express clinical priorities; the paper's second scheme gives
tolerability the most weight.  Re-weighting reuses the bootstrap fits, so
it is immediate:

```{r scheme2}
scheme2 <- update(modeled, weights = c(tox = 0.3, eff = 0.2, tol = 0.5))
scheme2$summary[, c("regimen", "est", "lower", "upper", "selFreq", "best")]
plot(scheme2, "endpoints")
```

`cuiSensitivity()` shows how far each weight can move before the
recommended dose changes:

```{r sensitivity}
plot(cuiSensitivity(modeled))
```

# Monotone fits

When biology says a probability can only rise (or fall) with dose, the
logistic models can be constrained.  `monotone` is about the raw
response, separately from `direction`; a flat fit is allowed:

```{r monotone}
monotone := cuiDoseResponse(trial,
  list(cuiBinary(tox, model = "exponential", direction = "lower", monotone = "increasing"),
       cuiBinary(eff, model = "logitQuadratic", monotone = "increasing"),
       cuiBinary(tol, model = "logitLinear", monotone = "increasing")),
  dose = dose, id = id, weights = c(tox = 0.2, eff = 0.5, tol = 0.3),
  nBoot = 1000, seed = 1, cacheDir = NA)
plot(monotone, "doseResponse")
```

# Your own model

Any fitted model of an endpoint works, for example a logistic regression
with a covariate.  It is averaged over the patients at each dose and refit
in every bootstrap sample.  `lme4`, `glmmTMB` and `brms` fits work the same
way, and other classes can be added with `cuiModelPredict()` methods.

```{r own-model}
trial$age <- round(runif(nrow(trial), 30, 75))
effGlm <- glm(eff ~ dose + I(dose^2) + age, family = binomial, data = trial)
own := cuiDoseResponse(trial,
  list(cuiBinary(tox, model = "exponential", direction = "lower"),
       cuiBinary(eff, model = effGlm),
       cuiBinary(tol, model = "logitLinear")),
  dose = dose, id = id, weights = c(tox = 0.2, eff = 0.5, tol = 0.3),
  nBoot = 1000, seed = 1, cacheDir = NA)
own$summary[, c("regimen", "est", "lower", "upper", "selFreq")]
```

# Interactive use

The same result opens in the desk tool, with weight sliders grouped into
efficacy and safety:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
cuiApp(modeled, presets = list("Scheme 1" = c(tox = 0.2, eff = 0.5, tol = 0.3),
                               "Scheme 2" = c(tox = 0.3, eff = 0.2, tol = 0.5)))
```
